title: Smallest ideal allowing a lift over a socle extension
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian ring and $k$ a field of finite type over $R$ [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], [def-weil-field], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Use the category $\mathcal C_{R,k}$ of Artinian local $R$-algebras with specified residue field $k$ and local maps inducing the identity on $k$ [def-sfb-artin-deformation-test-category]. Let $\mathcal F$ be a predeformation category on $\mathcal C_{R,k}$ satisfying (RS), as defined in [def-sfb-artin-deformation-test-category]. Let $B\twoheadrightarrow A$ be a morphism with kernel $I$ annihilated by $\mathfrak m_B$, and let $x\in\mathcal F(A)$. For an ideal $L\subseteq I$, call $L$ liftable if there are $y\in\mathcal F(B/L)$ and an isomorphism $y|_A\cong x$. The set of liftable ideals has a least member under inclusion, and this member is itself liftable.

proof.text: Write $\mathcal J$ for the set of liftable ideals. The kernel $I$ lies in $\mathfrak m_B$, since the given map induces the identity on residue fields. Every quotient $B/L$ for $L\subseteq I$ is a test algebra: inverse images identify its ideals with the ideals of $B$ containing $L$, so descending chains stabilize; its unique maximal ideal is $\mathfrak m_B/L$ and its residue field is $k$. The quotient maps are local and induce the identity on $k$. The map $B/I\to A$ is an isomorphism, so transport of $x$ along its inverse shows $I\in\mathcal J$. If $L\in\mathcal J$ and $L\subseteq L'\subseteq I$, transport along $B/L\to B/L'$ gives a lift whose restriction is still $x$, by the composition isomorphisms of the pseudofunctor.

source.place: Tag 06SZ (lemma-largest-closed-where-lift), proof; the displayed quotient formula has B in place of its typographical A.

proof.text: Take $J,K\in\mathcal J$. The action of $B$ on $I$ factors through $B/\mathfrak m_B=k$ because $\mathfrak m_BI=0$. Thus $I$ is a $k$-vector space, and its $B$-ideals are exactly its $k$-subspaces: a scalar acts by any representative in $B$. Apply the complement lemma to $J+K\subseteq I$, obtaining $I=(J+K)\oplus Q$. The subspace $J'=J+Q$ is an ideal, contains $J$, and satisfies $J'+K=I$. Also $J'\cap K=J\cap K$: if $j+q\in K$ with $j\in J$, $q\in Q$, then $q\in Q\cap(J+K)=0$. Step 1 shows that $J'$ is liftable.

source.place: Tag 06SZ (lemma-largest-closed-where-lift), proof; the displayed quotient formula has B in place of its typographical A.

proof.text: The natural homomorphism $\phi:B/(J'\cap K)\to(B/J')\times_A(B/K)$ sends $b$ to $(b\bmod J',b\bmod K)$. It is injective because its kernel before quotienting is $J'\cap K$. For surjectivity, represent a compatible pair by $b,c\in B$. Their images in $A$ agree, so $b-c\in I=J'+K$; write $b-c=j+u$ with $j\in J'$ and $u\in K$. Then $b-j=c+u$ represents both entries. These formulas prove that $\phi$ is an $R$-algebra isomorphism commuting with projections and residue maps, identifying the ring fibre product with the test algebra $B/(J'\cap K)$.

source.place: Tag 06SZ (lemma-largest-closed-where-lift), proof; the displayed quotient formula has B in place of its typographical A.

proof.text: Choose lifts $y\in\mathcal F(B/J')$, $z\in\mathcal F(B/K)$ and isomorphisms $a:y|_A\cong x$, $b:z|_A\cong x$. The triple $(y,z,b^{-1}\circ a)$ is an object of $\mathcal F(B/J')\times_{\mathcal F(A)}\mathcal F(B/K)$. The quotient $B/K\to A$ is surjective, so the (RS) equivalence in the cited definition applies. Essential surjectivity supplies an object over the fibre product with an isomorphism of its first projection to $y$. Via the ring isomorphism of step 3 this gives an object over $B/(J'\cap K)$. Restricting the projection isomorphism to $A$ and composing with $a$ identifies its restriction with $x$. Since $J'\cap K=J\cap K$, this proves $J\cap K\in\mathcal J$.

source.place: Tag 06SZ (lemma-largest-closed-where-lift), proof; the displayed quotient formula has B in place of its typographical A.

proof.text: The finite-length lemma supplies $N\geq0$ bounding the number of strict inclusions in every chain of ideals of $B$. Starting with $I\in\mathcal J$, replace the current member by a strictly smaller member of $\mathcal J$ whenever one exists. After at most $N$ replacements this stops at a minimal member $M\in\mathcal J$, since another replacement would give $N+1$ strict inclusions. For any $L\in\mathcal J$, step 4 makes $M\cap L$ a member of $\mathcal J$ contained in $M$. Minimality forces $M\cap L=M$, hence $M\subseteq L$. Thus $M$ is least, and is liftable because it belongs to $\mathcal J$.
